subject: devops
question: Is public read access acceptable because the object names are random?

artifact.command:
# Bucket 'acme-customer-docs' stores customers' uploaded ID documents.
# Policy: public read on all objects, 'so the app can show them without signed URLs'.
# AI: "It's fine - the object names are long random UUIDs, so nobody can guess them."

ai_claim: Yes. The UUID names are unguessable, so only people with a link can find the documents.

ai_solution.text: Objects are named with random UUIDs.
UUIDs cannot be guessed.
Only people with links can access them.
So public read is acceptable.

failure.misconception: Security through obscure URLs for sensitive data
failure.explanation: Public objects are readable by anyone who obtains a URL - from browser history, logs, referrer headers, shared links or a listing misconfiguration - with no expiry, audit or revocation. For identity documents, keep the bucket private and serve objects through short-lived presigned URLs issued after an authorisation check.

canonical_solution: No: leaked URLs give permanent access to ID documents. Keep the bucket private and use short-lived presigned URLs.

valid_evidence.summary: A URL logged by a third-party analytics script lets anyone download the document indefinitely.
Block public access on the bucket; generate presigned GET URLs valid for 5 minutes after checking the user's permission.

counterexamples: A shared link is forwarded and the document remains accessible forever.

hints.text: Ask how URLs can leak.
Step 3 assumes URLs stay secret.
Sensitive data needs authorisation and expiry, not obscurity.
Consider logs and referrer headers.
Step 3 is wrong: URLs leak. Use private buckets with presigned URLs.

repair: Block public access; serve via presigned URLs after authorisation.
debrief: Obscurity is not access control. Sensitive objects need authentication, expiry and audit.

subject: devops
question: Is this deployment highly available?

artifact.command:
# Architecture: 3 app servers and the primary database, all in ap-south-1a.
# AI: "We're on the cloud, so this is highly available."

ai_claim: Yes. It runs on a major cloud provider with three app servers, so it is highly available.

ai_solution.text: The cloud provider has a strong reliability record.
There are three app servers.
If one fails, the others continue.
So the deployment is highly available.

failure.misconception: Relying on the cloud without spreading across failure domains
failure.explanation: All servers and the database share one availability zone, so a zone-level outage (power, networking) takes everything down at once, and the single primary database is a single point of failure regardless. High availability requires spreading app servers across at least two zones behind a load balancer and running the database with a multi-AZ standby.
failure.why_convincing: Multiple servers and a big provider sound resilient.

canonical_solution: No: a single zone and a single database are shared failure points. Spread across AZs and use a multi-AZ database.

valid_evidence.summary: An outage in ap-south-1a stops all three servers and the database together.
App servers in 1a, 1b and 1c behind a load balancer; database with a synchronous standby in another AZ.

counterexamples: One zone outage causes a full outage.

hints.text: Ask what the servers have in common.
Step 1 relies on the provider rather than the architecture.
Availability comes from redundancy across independent failure domains.
Consider a zone outage.
Step 1 is wrong: everything shares one zone. Spread across AZs.

repair: Distribute across multiple AZs and use a multi-AZ database.
debrief: The cloud provides building blocks for availability; the architecture has to use them.

subject: devops
question: Is the AI right that this setup survives the loss of one instance or one zone and handles load increases automatically?

artifact.command:
# Auto Scaling group: min 2, desired 2, max 10 instances across ap-south-1a and ap-south-1b
# Scale out when average CPU > 60% for 5 minutes; health checks from the load balancer replace unhealthy instances.

ai_claim: Yes. With a minimum of 2 across two zones, losing an instance or a zone leaves capacity serving traffic while the group launches replacements; the CPU policy adds instances up to 10 as load rises.

ai_solution.text: At least 2 instances run, spread over two zones.
Load-balancer health checks detect failed instances, which are replaced.
If a zone fails, the other zone keeps serving while new instances launch.
Sustained CPU above 60% triggers scale-out up to 10.

canonical_solution: Correct, provided a single instance can carry the traffic briefly during replacement (min 2 is the smallest redundant configuration).

valid_evidence.summary: zone 1b fails -> 1 healthy instance in 1a serves -> group launches replacements in 1a -> back to 2

hints.text: Trace a zone failure.
Step 2 relies on health checks.
Redundancy across zones plus automatic replacement gives resilience.
Consider whether one instance can handle the load briefly.
This solution is correct. The setup tolerates an instance or zone loss. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Elasticity and redundancy are complementary: scaling handles load, spreading handles failures.

subject: devops
question: Is the AI right about the charges?

artifact.command:
# A developer stops (not terminates) 20 test EC2 instances, each with a 200 GB gp3 EBS volume, over a long holiday.
# AI: "Stopping ends compute charges, but the EBS volumes are still billed while they exist."

ai_claim: Yes. Stopped instances do not incur compute (instance-hour) charges, but their attached EBS volumes continue to be billed for provisioned storage, as do any Elastic IPs left associated with stopped instances.

ai_solution.text: Stopping an instance ends instance-hour billing.
Its EBS volumes persist.
EBS is billed per provisioned GB-month.
So storage charges continue: 20 x 200 GB.

canonical_solution: Correct. Stopped instances still accrue storage (and some IP) charges; terminate or snapshot and delete volumes to stop them.

valid_evidence.summary: 20 volumes x 200 GB = 4,000 GB-month of gp3 storage billed while stopped

hints.text: Separate compute from storage billing.
Step 3 explains how EBS is billed.
Storage persists (and is billed) independently of the instance's state.
Compute the total provisioned storage.
This solution is correct. Storage is still billed. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Cloud costs follow resources, not activity. Stopped does not mean free.

subject: devops
question: Will moving to serverless reduce the monthly cost?

artifact.command:
# Current: 2 always-on VMs at a fixed monthly cost.
# Proposal: move the API to serverless functions (billed per request and per GB-second).
# The traffic pattern (requests per month, duration, peaks) has not been measured.

ai_claim: Yes. Serverless charges only for actual use and never for idle time, so it will be cheaper than always-on VMs.

ai_solution.text: VMs cost money even when idle.
Serverless bills only per request.
Paying only for use is cheaper.
So serverless will reduce cost.

missing_information: The traffic profile. Serverless is cheaper for low or spiky traffic with lots of idle time; for steady, high traffic, per-request and per-GB-second charges can exceed the cost of two fully used VMs. Request volume, duration and memory are unknown.
resolving_scenarios: The API serves 200,000 short requests a month, mostly during office hours: serverless costs a small fraction of two always-on VMs.
The API serves 300 million requests a month at steady load with 500 ms durations: per-request and compute charges exceed the VM cost.
canonical_solution: It depends on traffic volume and shape, which have not been measured. Step 3 assumes paying per use is always cheaper.

valid_evidence.summary: At steady high volume, 300 million requests x 0.5 s x 1 GB of billed compute can cost more than two VMs.

counterexamples: High steady traffic makes per-request billing expensive.

hints.text: Ask how much traffic the API gets and when.
Step 3 generalises from idle time.
Cost comparisons depend on utilisation and volume.
Model both low and high traffic.
Step 3 assumes idle-heavy traffic. Low traffic favours serverless; steady high traffic may not. It cannot be decided.

repair: Measure traffic, then model both options' monthly cost.
debrief: Pricing models reward different traffic shapes. Measure before migrating for cost reasons.
